summary.text: Take the prime \(p=41\): since \(-30\equiv11\pmod{41}\) and \(11^{20}\equiv-1\pmod{41}\), one has \(\left(\frac{-30}{41}\right)=-1\). Direct finite evaluation of the defining sum gives \(S(41)\equiv899\not\equiv0\pmod{41^2}\), contradicting the first asserted congruence.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
T_k(b,c)=[x^k](x^2+bx+c)^k
\]
be the generalized central trinomial coefficient. We will disprove part (1) of the conjecture by taking the prime
\[
p=41.
\]
The modulus in the conjecture is then
\[
p^2=41^2=1681.
\]
We will show both that
\[
\left(\frac{-30}{41}\right)=-1
\]
and that
\[
S(41)\equiv 899\not\equiv 0\pmod{1681}.
\]
These two facts directly contradict part (1).

First, recall an explicit formula for the coefficients. To obtain a term of degree exactly \(k\) in \((x^2+bx+c)^k\), suppose that \(i\) of the \(k\) factors contribute \(x^2\), another \(i\) factors contribute \(c\), and the remaining \(k-2i\) factors contribute \(bx\). The resulting degree is
\[
2i+(k-2i)=k.
\]
Consequently
\[
T_k(b,c)=\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor k/2\rfloor}
 \binom{k}{i}\binom{k-i}{i}b^{k-2i}c^i.
\tag{1}
\]
In particular, all the quantities used below are integers.

For completeness, it is useful to derive a short recurrence that makes the finite calculation reproducible. The generating function of these generalized central trinomial coefficients is
\[
G(t):=\sum_{n\geq 0}T_n(b,c)t^n
 =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-2bt+(b^2-4c)t^2}}.
\tag{2}
\]
One way to see this is to regard \(T_n(b,c)\) as the constant term of \((x+b+c/x)^n\). Summing the resulting geometric series and extracting its constant term gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
G(t)
&=\operatorname{CT}_x\frac{1}{1-t(x+b+c/x)}\\
&=\sum_{j\geq0}\binom{2j}{j}
   \frac{c^j t^{2j}}{(1-bt)^{2j+1}}\\
&=\frac1{1-bt}\left(1-\frac{4ct^2}{(1-bt)^2}\right)^{-1/2}\\
&=\frac1{\sqrt{(1-bt)^2-4ct^2}},
\end{aligned}
\]
which is (2).

Put \(d=b^2-4c\). Differentiating (2) gives
\[
(1-2bt+dt^2)G'(t)=(b-dt)G(t).
\]
Equating coefficients of \(t^{n-1}\), for \(n\geq2\), yields
\[
nT_n(b,c)
=b(2n-1)T_{n-1}(b,c)-d(n-1)T_{n-2}(b,c).
\tag{3}
\]
The initial values are
\[
T_0(b,c)=1,\qquad T_1(b,c)=b.
\]
For the present calculation \(c=81\), so \(d=b^2-324\). Thus (3), specialized to \(b=2\) and \(b=14\), together with the initial values, computes all the needed values of \(T_k(2,81)\) and \(T_k(14,81)\). Formula (1) is also a direct independent description of every entry.

We now compute the sum
\[
S(41)=\sum_{k=0}^{40}\binom{2k}{k}T_k(2,81)T_k(14,81)
\]
modulo \(1681\). In the following table, every entry is represented by its least nonnegative residue modulo \(1681\). The columns headed \(T_2\) and \(T_{14}\) mean respectively \(T_k(2,81)\) and \(T_k(14,81)\). The column \(C\) is \(\binom{2k}{k}\), the column \(A_k\) is the complete summand
\[
A_k=\binom{2k}{k}T_k(2,81)T_k(14,81),
\]
and the last column is the running sum \(A_0+\cdots+A_k\). All columns are reduced modulo \(1681\).

\[

Here the two \(T\)-columns may be obtained successively from recurrence (3). The central binomial column is obtained from \(C_k=\binom{2k}{k}\), or successively from the exact identity
\[
k^2 C_k=(2k)(2k-1)C_{k-1},\qquad C_0=1.
\]
Multiplying the three relevant entries gives the summand column, and ordinary modular addition gives the final column. Thus the final entry proves
\[
S(41)\equiv899\pmod{1681}.
\tag{4}
\]
Since \(0<899<1681\), this residue is not zero. Hence
\[
S(41)\not\equiv0\pmod{41^2}.
\tag{5}
\]

It remains to verify that this prime satisfies the hypothesis in part (1). First, \(41\) is prime: it has no prime divisor at most \(\sqrt{41}<7\), since it is divisible by none of \(2,3,5\). It also satisfies \(41>7\).

Modulo \(41\),
\[
-30\equiv11.
\]
We can check that \(11\) is a quadratic nonresidue by Euler's criterion. Indeed,
\[
11^2=121\equiv-2\pmod{41},
\]
so
\[
11^4\equiv4\pmod{41}.
\]
It follows that
\[
11^{20}=(11^4)^5\equiv4^5=1024\equiv40\equiv-1\pmod{41},
\]
because \(1024-24\cdot41=40\). Euler's criterion therefore gives
\[
\left(\frac{11}{41}\right)=-1.
\]
As \(-30\equiv11\pmod{41}\), the Legendre symbol depends only on the residue class, and hence
\[
\left(\frac{-30}{41}\right)=-1.
\tag{6}
\]

Part (1) of the conjecture asserts that for every prime \(p>7\), the condition
\(\left(\frac{-30}{p}\right)=-1\) implies
\[
S(p)\equiv0\pmod{p^2}.
\]
For \(p=41\), the primality and size requirements hold and (6) verifies the Legendre-symbol hypothesis. The asserted conclusion would therefore be
\[
S(41)\equiv0\pmod{1681}.
\]
But (4) and (5) show instead that its residue is \(899\), which is nonzero. Thus part (1), and consequently the conjunction constituting Conjecture 3, is false.
